notes.front: What is a stairrail system, in Subpart X?
notes.back: A vertical barrier along the unprotected sides and edges of a stairway, to prevent employees from falling to lower levels.
notes.explanation: Its top surface can double as the handrail, so one rail may serve both purposes.
notes.example: Like the rail and infill panels down the open side of a timber site stair between two storeys of a new block of flats.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1050(b), p. 521
notes.evidence: Stairrail system means a vertical barrier erected along the unprotected sides and edges of a stariway to prevent employees from falling to lower levels. The top surface of a stairrail system may also be a ‘‘handrail.’’

notes.front: What is a portable ladder, in Subpart X?
notes.back: A ladder that can be readily moved or carried.
notes.explanation: Mobility is the whole test: the definition says nothing about the ladder's material, length or design.
notes.example: Like the extension ladder a roofer carries from the van to the gable end, as opposed to steel rungs built into a lift shaft wall.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1050(b), p. 521
notes.evidence: Portable ladder means a ladder that can be readily moved or carried.

notes.front: What is a fixed ladder, in Subpart X?
notes.back: A ladder that cannot be readily moved or carried because it is an integral part of a building or structure.
notes.explanation: Fixed ladders come in side-step and through types; on a side-step ladder the climber steps to the side of the rails to reach the landing at the top.
notes.example: Like the steel rung ladder welded up the side of a storage silo, rather than a stepladder folded and moved between rooms.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1050(b), p. 520
notes.evidence: Fixed ladder means a ladder that cannot be readily moved or carried because it is an integral part of a building or structure. A side-step fixed ladder is a fixed ladder that requires a person getting off at the top to step to the side of the ladder side rails to reach the landing.

notes.front: A stairway or ladder must be provided at all personnel points of access where there is a break in elevation of {{c1::19 inches (48 cm)}} or more, and no ramp, runway, sloped embankment or personnel hoist is provided.
notes.explanation: A ramp, runway, sloped embankment or personnel hoist also meets the rule; only where none of them is provided does a stairway or ladder have to be added.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1051(a), p. 521
notes.evidence: A stairway or ladder shall be provided at all personnel points of access where there is a break in elevation of 19 inches (48 cm) or more, and no ramp, runway, sloped embankment, or personnel hoist is provided.

notes.front: When must a double-cleated ladder, or two or more separate ladders, be provided?
notes.back: When ladders are the only access to or exit from a work area for 25 or more employees, or a ladder serves simultaneous two-way traffic.
notes.explanation: In either case a single ladder is not enough; the rule accepts a double-cleated ladder or separate ladders as alternatives.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1051(a)(2), p. 521
notes.evidence: A double-cleated ladder or two or more separate ladders shall be provided when ladders are the only mean of access or exit from a working area for 25 or more employees, or when a ladder is to serve simultaneous two-way traffic.

notes.front: Which stairways must have at least one handrail and a stairrail system along each unprotected side or edge?
notes.back: Those with four or more risers, or rising more than 30 inches (76 cm), whichever is less.
notes.explanation: "Whichever is less" means a flight can come under the rule by its rise alone, before it reaches four risers.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1052(c)(1), p. 522
notes.evidence: Stairways having four or more risers or rising more than 30 inches (76 cm), whichever is less, shall be equipped with: (i) At least one handrail; and (ii) One stairrail system along each unprotected side or edge.

notes.front: How high must a stairrail installed after 15 March 1991 be?
notes.back: At least 36 inches (91.5 cm) from its upper surface to the tread, in line with the riser face at the tread's forward edge.
notes.explanation: Stairrails installed before that date follow an older range with a lower minimum of 30 inches, so the installation date decides which height applies.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1052(c)(3), p. 522
notes.evidence: Stairrails installed after March 15, 1991, shall be not less than 36 inches (91.5 cm) from the upper surface of the stairrail system to the surface of the tread, in line with the face of the riser at the forward edge of the tread. (ii) Stairrails installed before March 15, 1991, shall be not less than 30 inches

notes.front: When a portable ladder is used for access to an upper landing surface, its side rails must extend at least {{c1::3 feet (.9 m)}} above that landing surface.
notes.explanation: The use rules in § 1926.1053(b), this one included, apply to all ladders, job-made ladders among them, unless a rule says otherwise.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1053(b)(1), p. 526
notes.evidence: (b) Use. The following requirements apply to the use of all ladders, including job-made ladders, except as otherwise indicated: (1) When portable ladders are used for access to an upper landing surface, the ladder side rails shall extend at least 3 feet (.9 m) above the upper landing surface

notes.front: A portable ladder is too short to extend the required distance above the landing it serves. What must be done instead?
notes.back: Secure its top to a rigid support that will not deflect, and provide a grasping device, such as a grabrail, for getting on and off.
notes.explanation: The extension must never be such that the ladder's deflection under a load could by itself make it slip off its support.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1053(b)(1), p. 526
notes.evidence: secured at its top to a rigid support that will not deflect, and a grasping device, such as a grabrail, shall be provided to assist employees in mounting and dismounting the ladder. In no case shall the extension be such that ladder deflection under a load would, by itself, cause the ladder to slip off its support.

notes.front: A non-self-supporting ladder must be used at an angle where the horizontal distance from the top support to the foot is approximately {{c1::one-quarter}} of the ladder's working length.
notes.explanation: Working length is the distance along the ladder between its foot and the top support, which is the figure the fraction is taken of.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1053(b)(5)(i), p. 526
notes.evidence: Non-self-supporting ladders shall be used at an angle such that the horizontal distance from the top support to the foot of the ladder is approximately one-quarter of the working length of the ladder (the distance along the ladder between the foot and the top support).

notes.front: At what angle must a wood job-made ladder with spliced side rails be used?
notes.back: So that the horizontal distance is one-eighth of the ladder's working length.
notes.explanation: One-eighth puts the ladder more upright than the approximately one-quarter set for other non-self-supporting ladders.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1053(b)(5)(ii), p. 526
notes.evidence: is approximately one-quarter of the working length of the ladder (the distance along the ladder between the foot and the top support). (ii) Wood job-made ladders with spliced side rails shall be used at an angle such that the horizontal distance is one-eighth the working length of the ladder.

notes.front: What load must a self-supporting portable ladder support without failure?
notes.back: At least four times its maximum intended load; an extra-heavy-duty type 1A metal or plastic ladder, at least 3.3 times.
notes.explanation: The rule sets a margin over the expected load rather than a fixed weight, and only one class of ladder gets the lower factor.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1053(a)(1)(i), p. 523
notes.evidence: Each self-supporting portable ladder: At least four times the maximum intended load, except that each extraheavy-duty type 1A metal or plastic ladder shall sustain at least 3.3 times

notes.front: Rungs, cleats and steps of most portable ladders and of fixed ladders must be spaced not less than 10 inches and not more than {{c1::14 inches}} apart, measured between centre lines.
notes.explanation: They must also be parallel, level and uniformly spaced when the ladder is in position for use.
notes.evidence: (2) Ladder rungs, cleats, and steps shall be parallel, level, and uniformly spaced when the ladder is in position for use. (3)(i) Rungs, cleats, and steps of portable ladders (except as provided below) and fixed ladders (including individualrung/step ladders) shall be spaced not less than 10 inches (25 cm) apart, nor more than 14 inches (36 cm) apart

notes.front: When must a ladder have nonconductive side rails?
notes.back: When it is used where the employee or the ladder could contact exposed energised electrical equipment.
notes.explanation: Contact by the ladder itself counts as much as contact by the person on it; § 1926.955(b) and (c) set the only exceptions.
notes.evidence: employee or the ladder could contact exposed energized electrical equipment, except as provided in § 1926.955(b) and (c) of this part.

notes.front: The {{c1::top or top step}} of a stepladder must not be used as a step.
notes.explanation: The next rule adds that a stepladder's rear cross-bracing is not for climbing either, unless the ladder has steps on both sections.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1053(b)(13), p. 527
notes.evidence: (13) The top or top step of a stepladder shall not be used as a step. (14) Cross-bracing on the rear section of stepladders shall not be used for climbing unless the ladders are designed and provided with steps for climbing on both front and rear sections.

notes.front: When may the cross-bracing on the rear section of a stepladder be climbed?
notes.back: Only when the ladder is designed and provided with steps for climbing on both front and rear sections.
notes.explanation: The exception turns on how the ladder was built: without steps on the rear section, the bracing is not a climbing surface.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1053(b)(14), p. 527
notes.evidence: Cross-bracing on the rear section of stepladders shall not be used for climbing unless the ladders are designed and provided with steps for climbing on both front and rear sections.

notes.front: When going up or down a ladder, which way must the user face, and how many hands must grasp the ladder?
notes.back: Face the ladder, and grasp it with at least one hand while moving up or down.
notes.explanation: A third rule in the same list bars carrying any object or load that could make the employee lose balance and fall.
notes.evidence: (20) When ascending or descending a ladder, the user shall face the ladder. (21) Each employee shall use at least one hand to grasp the ladder when progressing up and/or down the ladder. (22) An employee shall not carry any object or load that could cause the employee to lose balance and fall.

notes.front: What must an employee not carry on a ladder?
notes.back: Any object or load that could cause the employee to lose balance and fall.
notes.explanation: The test is the effect on the climber's balance; the rule names no weight or size limit.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1053(b)(22), p. 527
notes.evidence: An employee shall not carry any object or load that could cause the employee to lose balance and fall.

notes.front: Ladders must be inspected by a {{c1::competent person}} for visible defects on a periodic basis and after any occurrence that could affect their safe use.
notes.explanation: The duty has two triggers: a regular cycle, and any event that might have affected the ladder in between.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1053(b)(15), p. 527
notes.evidence: Ladders shall be inspected by a competent person for visible defects on a periodic basis and after any occurrence that could affect their safe use.

notes.front: What must happen to a portable ladder with a structural defect, such as a broken rung or a split rail?
notes.back: Mark it at once as defective, or tag it ‘Do Not Use’ or similar, and withdraw it from service until repaired.
notes.explanation: The listed defects are examples only: corroded components and other faulty or defective components count too.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1053(b)(16), p. 527
notes.evidence: structural defects, such as, but not limited to, broken or missing rungs, cleats, or steps, broken or split rails, corroded components, or other faulty or defective components, shall either be immediately marked in a manner that readily identifies them as defective, or be tagged with ‘‘Do Not Use’’ or similar language, and shall be withdrawn from service until repaired.

notes.front: On what kind of surface may a ladder be used without being secured against accidental displacement?
notes.back: A stable and level one; on any other surface it must be secured.
notes.explanation: On slippery surfaces slip-resistant feet are allowed, but they are no substitute for care in placing, lashing or holding the ladder.
notes.evidence: (6) Ladders shall be used only on stable and level surfaces unless secured to prevent accidental displacement. (7) Ladders shall not be used on slippery surfaces unless secured or provided with slip-resistant feet to prevent accidental displacement. Slip-resistant feet shall not be used as a substitute for care in placing, lashing, or holding a ladder

notes.front: A fixed ladder's total climb is 24 feet or more. What are two of the options it may be equipped with?
notes.back: Any two of: ladder safety devices; self-retracting lifelines with rest platforms at most 150 feet apart; a cage or well with multiple ladder sections.
notes.explanation: One option is enough, and the cage-or-well option also limits each ladder section to 50 feet.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1053(a)(19), p. 525
notes.evidence: fixed ladders shall be equipped with one of the following: (i) Ladder safety devices; or (ii) Self-retracting lifelines, and rest platforms at intervals not to exceed 150 feet (45.7 m); or (iii) A cage or well, and multiple ladder sections, each ladder section not to exceed 50 feet (15.2 m) in length.

notes.front: What are two areas in which a competent person must train each employee who uses ladders and stairways?
notes.back: Any two of: fall hazards in the work area; fall protection system procedures; proper construction, use, placement and care of stairways and ladders.
notes.explanation: The areas apply as applicable, so each employee is trained in the ones that fit the work they do.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1060(a)(1), p. 527
notes.evidence: each employee has been trained by a competent person in the following areas, as applicable: (i) The nature of fall hazards in the work area; (ii) The correct procedures for erecting, maintaining, and disassembling the fall protection systems to be used; (iii) The proper construction, use, placement, and care in handling of all stairways and ladders

notes.front: Formwork carpenters step up 20 inches from a deck to a raised slab many times a day. No ramp, runway, sloped embankment or personnel hoist is provided. What does Subpart X require at that point of access?
notes.choices:
A) A stairway or ladder
B) Nothing, because the step is under 24 inches
C) A guardrail system along the slab edge
D) A sign warning of the step
notes.back: A: a stairway or ladder.
notes.choicesExplained: B: the threshold is 19 inches, not 24. C: a guardrail system is fall protection, not a way up between levels. D: a warning sign is not one of the means the rule accepts.
notes.explanation: 20 inches is above the 19-inch break in elevation, and none of the four alternatives the rule allows is provided.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1051(a), p. 521
notes.evidence: A stairway or ladder shall be provided at all personnel points of access where there is a break in elevation of 19 inches (48 cm) or more, and no ramp, runway, sloped embankment, or personnel hoist is provided.

notes.front: A temporary stair has three risers that together rise 33 inches, with one open side. Does it need a handrail and a stairrail system?
notes.back: Yes. It rises more than 30 inches, and that trigger is reached before four risers, so both are required.
notes.explanation: The rule applies at four risers or more than 30 inches, whichever is less, so the rise alone brings this stair under it.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1052(c)(1), p. 522
notes.evidence: Stairways having four or more risers or rising more than 30 inches (76 cm), whichever is less, shall be equipped with: (i) At least one handrail; and (ii) One stairrail system along each unprotected side or edge.

notes.front: An electrician leans an extension ladder against a building to climb onto its flat roof. The ladder is long enough. How far above the roof surface must its side rails extend?
notes.choices:
A) 12 inches
B) At least 3 feet
C) Level with the roof edge
D) 2 feet
notes.back: B: at least 3 feet (.9 m).
notes.choicesExplained: A and D fall short of the 3-foot minimum. C gives no extension at all, which the rule allows only through its alternative for ladders too short to extend.
notes.explanation: An extension ladder is a portable ladder, and here it gives access to an upper landing surface, so the 3-foot extension applies.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1053(b)(1), p. 526
notes.evidence: When portable ladders are used for access to an upper landing surface, the ladder side rails shall extend at least 3 feet (.9 m) above the upper landing surface to which the ladder is used to gain access; or, when such an extension is not possible because of the ladder’s length

notes.front: A manufactured straight ladder has a working length of 16 feet between its foot and the top support. About how far, measured horizontally, should its foot be from the top support?
notes.choices:
A) About 4 feet
B) About 2 feet
C) About 8 feet
D) Right against the wall
notes.back: A: about 4 feet.
notes.choicesExplained: B is one-eighth, the figure for wood job-made ladders with spliced side rails. C is one-half, far too shallow. D gives no horizontal distance at all.
notes.explanation: One-quarter of a 16-foot working length is 4 feet.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1053(b)(5), p. 526
notes.evidence: is approximately one-quarter of the working length of the ladder (the distance along the ladder between the foot and the top support). (ii) Wood job-made ladders with spliced side rails shall be used at an angle such that the horizontal distance is one-eighth the working length of the ladder.

notes.front: A worker must set up a portable ladder to fix a sign beside an exposed, energised conductor, and the ladder could touch it. Which ladder may be used?
notes.choices:
A) Any ladder, if the worker wears gloves
B) A ladder with nonconductive side rails
C) A metal ladder with slip-resistant feet
D) A metal ladder tied off at the top
notes.back: B: a ladder with nonconductive side rails.
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule is about the ladder's side rails, and gloves do not change that. C: slip-resistant feet deal with slipping, not electrical contact. D: securing a metal ladder does not make its rails nonconductive.
notes.explanation: The ladder could contact exposed energised electrical equipment, which is exactly when the rule requires nonconductive side rails.
notes.evidence: employee or the ladder could contact exposed energized electrical equipment, except as provided in § 1926.955(b) and (c) of this part.

notes.front: A decorator on a stepladder stands on its top step for a few seconds to reach a ceiling corner. Is that allowed?
notes.back: No. The top step of a stepladder must not be used as a step, however brief the task.
notes.explanation: The rule gives no exception for short reaches, so the length of the task does not matter.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1053(b)(13), p. 527
notes.evidence: (13) The top or top step of a stepladder shall not be used as a step.

notes.front: A labourer climbs down a ladder facing outwards, holding a box of fittings in both hands. Which statement is right?
notes.choices:
A) It is fine if the box is light
B) It is fine if another worker holds the ladder
C) It breaks the rules to face the ladder and to grasp it with at least one hand
D) It breaks only the rule on carrying loads
notes.back: C: it breaks the rules to face the ladder and to grasp it with at least one hand.
notes.choicesExplained: A: however light the box, no hand is on the ladder and the climber faces away. B: someone holding the ladder does not satisfy either rule. D: facing away and having no hand on the ladder break two other rules as well.
notes.explanation: Facing outwards breaks the facing rule, and both hands on the box leave none to grasp the ladder.
notes.evidence: (20) When ascending or descending a ladder, the user shall face the ladder. (21) Each employee shall use at least one hand to grasp the ladder when progressing up and/or down the ladder.

notes.front: On a periodic check, a competent person finds a portable ladder with a split side rail. The crew needs it later today. What must happen?
notes.choices:
A) Use it with extra care until the end of the week
B) Mark or tag it as defective and withdraw it from service until repaired
C) Keep using it for short climbs only
D) Lend it to a trade doing lighter work
notes.back: B: mark or tag it as defective and withdraw it from service until repaired.
notes.choicesExplained: A, D and C all keep a defective ladder in service, which the rule forbids until it is repaired.
notes.explanation: A split rail is one of the structural defects the rule lists, and the crew's need for the ladder makes no difference.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1053(b)(16), p. 527
notes.evidence: structural defects, such as, but not limited to, broken or missing rungs, cleats, or steps, broken or split rails, corroded components, or other faulty or defective components, shall either be immediately marked in a manner that readily identifies them as defective, or be tagged with ‘‘Do Not Use’’ or similar language, and shall be withdrawn from service until repaired.

notes.front: Before a new hire's first ladder job, the employer hands over the ladder maker's leaflet and nothing more. What does the Subpart X training rule require instead?
notes.back: Training by a competent person in the applicable areas, such as fall hazards in the work area and proper ladder use and placement.
notes.explanation: A leaflet is not training by a competent person, and the employer must ensure each employee who uses ladders has had that training.
notes.source: 29 CFR Part 1926 (revised as of 1 July 2025), § 1926.1060(a)(1), p. 527
notes.evidence: each employee has been trained by a competent person in the following areas, as applicable: (i) The nature of fall hazards in the work area; (ii) The correct procedures for erecting, maintaining, and disassembling the fall protection systems to be used; (iii) The proper construction, use, placement, and care in handling of all stairways and ladders
